exact_trigger_conflicts.printed: One role focused much more on running the work and reported to a Senior Director. Another led a transformation office and worked directly with a Chief Transformation Officer. Same broad title level. Very different job. The title can start the search. It cannot finish the read.
exact_trigger_conflicts.actual: Next, look at the verbs. Does the person decide? Lead? Negotiate? Recommend? Influence? Support? Execute?

exact_trigger_conflicts.printed: Those four things help you answer three different questions: Could I do this work? Can I prove that I have done something close to it? Do I meet the real requirements? Those are not the same question.
exact_trigger_conflicts.actual: The win is not becoming perfect at reading job descriptions. In ten minutes, name the problem, authority, proof, and real gap. That is enough to decide whether the role deserves a deeper look.

exact_trigger_conflicts.printed: That is why I think the worst time to reconstruct your career evidence is after you lose access to it. And no, I am not telling you to take company files. I am going to show you what to capture while you still have access, and how to do it without taking anything that belongs to your employer.
exact_trigger_conflicts.actual: Once a month, take ten minutes and write down: What changed? What was mine?

exact_trigger_conflicts.printed: And if you want to know what to capture before a layoff or sudden exit takes that access away, watch “Before a Layoff, Know What You Can Still Prove” next.
exact_trigger_conflicts.actual: That is why keeping career evidence is not only something to do when you think a layoff is coming. It is a normal career habit.

exact_trigger_conflicts.printed: I would make four columns: What travels? What does not? What can I prove? What must I relearn? Because changing industries without starting over does not mean pretending you have nothing left to learn.
exact_trigger_conflicts.actual: Ask: What travels? What does not? What can I prove? What must I relearn?
